summary: A Calm blog article, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, explaining why humans dream and how dreams relate to emotions, memory, sleep cycles and nightmares. It covers the theories that dreams help process emotions, consolidate memories and rehearse threats, describes REM and non-REM dreaming, and argues dreams don't disrupt sleep except through nightmares. It ends with five strategies to reduce nightmares and FAQs on dream realism, forgetting, pain, recall and duration.
one_line: Calm blog article explaining the purpose of dreams, how sleep cycles shape dreaming, how nightmares affect sleep, and five ways to reduce them.
key_facts: Humans spend about two hours a night dreaming, yet often don't remember most of their dreams.
Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.
Dreams may help the brain process emotions experienced during the day, making problems less daunting after a good night's sleep.
The theory is that dreams help organize information acquired during the day as the brain decides whether each experience is a memory to keep or let fade away.
Early human ancestors may have used dreams to practice real-life scenarios like escaping a wild beast or finding shelter in a storm.
Throughout the night the brain cycles through sleep stages, each lasting around 90 minutes.
REM typically starts about 70 to 90 minutes after a person first falls asleep.
During REM sleep the brain is nearly as active as when awake, so dreams are most vivid and story-like.
Neurotransmitters like serotonin and hormones like melatonin and cortisol play a role in shaping dreams.
Contrary to popular belief, dreaming doesn't disrupt sleep; nightmares are the exception.
Nightmares often reflect stress, fears, or underlying psychological concerns and are common in childhood but adults can have them too.
Common nightmare triggers include daytime stress from work pressures, relationship issues, or global events, and past traumas.
Going to bed and waking at the same time, even at weekends, can help regulate sleep and reduce nightmares.
Dream duration can range from a few seconds to about 20-30 minutes, typically increasing with each REM cycle, with the longest dreams occurring towards morning.
It is rare to feel physical pain in dreams because the brain's pain receptors aren't active during sleep.
